subsection: 2. Using the kinetic theory: separation techniques

notes.h: Explaining the properties of the states
notes.b: The kinetic theory says matter is made of particles that are always moving. How close the particles are, how strongly they attract one another and how they move explain why solids, liquids and gases behave so differently.
points: Solids have a fixed shape and volume and cannot be compressed (squeezed into a smaller volume), because the particles are held tightly in fixed positions by strong forces and only vibrate on the spot.
Liquids have a fixed volume but take the shape of their container and flow, because the particles are close together but can slide past one another.

Gases fill their container and are easily compressed, because the particles are far apart, with weak forces between them, and move rapidly and randomly. The empty space between them is what lets them be pushed closer.
Gas pressure is caused by gas particles colliding with the walls of the container. Many fast collisions every second add up to a steady push on the walls.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to explain properties and changes of state in terms of particles, so always name the particle arrangement, movement and forces, not just the property.

notes.b: Each change of state is explained by the energy of the particles and the forces between them. Heating gives particles energy to break free of those forces, and cooling takes energy away so the forces win again.
points: Melting (solid to liquid): heating makes the particles vibrate more until they have enough energy to overcome some of the forces holding them in place and begin to move past one another. This happens at the melting point.
Freezing (liquid to solid): cooling removes energy, the particles slow down, and the forces pull them back into fixed positions.
Evaporation (liquid to gas, below the boiling point): the fastest-moving particles at the surface escape, and because the fastest (highest-energy) particles leave, the remaining liquid cools.

Boiling (liquid to gas at the boiling point): particles throughout the liquid have enough energy to overcome the forces between them, so bubbles of vapour (the substance as a gas) form within the liquid.
Condensation (gas to liquid): cooling slows the particles so that the attractive forces pull them close together.
Sublimation (solid to gas directly, without melting), e.g. iodine, and solid carbon dioxide (“dry ice”), which sublimes at atmospheric pressure at −78 °C.
Deposition (gas to solid directly) is the reverse of sublimation, e.g. iodine vapour forming crystals on a cold surface.
Diagram: a triangle of the three states with arrows labelled melting, freezing, evaporation and boiling, condensation, sublimation and deposition.
notes.tip: Boiling and evaporation are different: evaporation happens from the surface at any temperature, while boiling happens throughout the liquid at the boiling point.

notes.b: A heating curve plots temperature against time as a pure substance is heated at a steady rate. The flat sections show the changes of state, and they show where the supplied energy goes.
points: When a pure solid is heated at a steady rate, its temperature rises until it reaches the melting point, then stays constant until it has all melted.

During a change of state the energy supplied is used to overcome the forces between particles, not to increase their kinetic energy (the energy of their movement), so the temperature does not rise even though heat is being supplied.
The temperature then rises again until the boiling point, where it stays constant until all the liquid has boiled.
The boiling plateau (flat section) is longer than the melting plateau because far more energy is needed to separate the particles completely than to loosen them.

Diagram: a heating curve for water (temperature against time) from ice below 0 °C to steam above 100 °C, with the two flat sections labelled melting at 0 °C and boiling at 100 °C. Water melts at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C at standard pressure.
notes.tip: You are asked to interpret a heating curve and explain the flat sections. Say that the temperature is constant during a change of state even though heat is being supplied, because the energy is used to overcome forces between particles.

notes.h: Assumptions of the model (Higher Level only)
notes.b: The kinetic theory is a model, a simplified picture of reality. The assumptions below are what the model takes to be true about gas particles.
points: Assumption: the particles are tiny spheres in constant, random motion.
Assumption: the higher the temperature, the greater the average kinetic energy (energy of movement) of the particles.
Assumption: collisions between particles are perfectly elastic, which means no kinetic energy is lost when they collide.
Assumption: in a gas the volume of the particles themselves is negligible (so small it can be ignored), and there are no forces between the particles except during collisions.
notes.tip: You may be asked to give the assumptions of the kinetic theory. Keep assumptions and limitations separate, and give them in the Higher Level answer only.

notes.h: Limitations: forces and identical particles (Higher Level only)
notes.b: A model is useful only if you know where it fails. The first two limitations come from what the simple model leaves out about the forces between particles.
points: Limitation: real particles are not hard spheres, and they do attract one another. These forces between particles (intermolecular forces) are what make liquids and solids exist and decide melting and boiling points, which the simple gas model ignores.

Limitation: the model treats all particles as identical, so it does not explain why different substances have different melting and boiling points. That needs the types of bonding and intermolecular forces. There is more on this in Polarity, shape and physical properties.

notes.h: Limitations: particle structure and real gases (Higher Level only)
notes.b: The model also says nothing about what is inside particles, and it works best only for gases under certain conditions.
points: Limitation: the model does not describe the structure inside particles or what happens to bonds, and it is qualitative (it describes behaviour in words), giving no values.

Limitation: in real gases at high pressure or low temperature the particles' volume and attractions matter, because the particles are then squeezed close together or moving slowly, so gases deviate from the model. There is more on this in Gas laws and the ideal gas equation.
notes.tip: If asked for two assumptions and one limitation, take the two assumptions from the assumptions block and one limitation from either limitations block.

notes.b: A mixture is separated by using a physical property in which its components differ. So the first step is always to work out how the components differ, then choose the technique that uses that difference.
points: Particle size and solubility (whether a substance dissolves) separate by filtration; solubility and volatility (how easily a substance turns to vapour) by evaporation and crystallisation; boiling point by distillation.
Solubility in a solvent and attraction to paper separate by chromatography; immiscibility (the liquids do not mix) and density by a separating funnel.

Heterogeneous mixtures (the components can be seen as separate parts), such as an insoluble solid in a liquid or two immiscible liquids, are separated by filtration, decanting (carefully pouring off the liquid) or a separating funnel.
Homogeneous mixtures (uniform throughout), such as solutions and miscible liquids (liquids that mix completely), need evaporation, crystallisation, distillation or chromatography.
notes.tip: You are asked to choose and justify a technique for a given mixture. Name the property the components differ in, then give the technique that uses it.

notes.b: Filtration separates an insoluble solid (one that does not dissolve) from a liquid. The paper has holes small enough to hold back the solid particles but large enough to let the liquid through.
points: Example: sand is separated from salt solution by filtration, because sand is insoluble and the salt is dissolved in the water.
Step 1: Fold filter paper into a cone and place it in a funnel.
Step 2: Pour the mixture through the filter paper; the solid (residue) stays on the paper and the liquid (filtrate) passes through.
Diagram: filter funnel with filter paper over a conical flask, labelled residue and filtrate.

notes.b: When a solid is dissolved in a liquid, filtering will not work because the dissolved solid passes through the paper. Instead you remove the solvent (the liquid that does the dissolving) by heating, either completely (evaporation) or only partly (crystallisation).
points: Evaporation recovers a dissolved solid by heating the solution until all the solvent has gone, e.g. salt from salt water. It is used when the solid does not decompose (break down) on heating.
Step 1 of crystallisation: Heat the solution to evaporate some solvent until it is saturated (cannot dissolve any more solid). A drop on a cold glass rod forms crystals when it is saturated.
Step 2 of crystallisation: Leave the solution to cool slowly so that crystals form, e.g. copper(II) sulfate crystals.
Step 3 of crystallisation: Filter off the crystals, wash them with a little cold solvent and dry them.
Crystallisation gives purer, larger crystals than evaporating to dryness, because soluble impurities stay in the solution.

notes.b: Distillation separates a liquid from a solution, or two liquids with different boiling points, by boiling and condensing the vapour. The liquid with the lower boiling point boils off first and is collected separately.
points: Simple distillation separates a solvent from a solution, or two liquids with very different boiling points, e.g. pure water from salt water.
Step 1: Heat the mixture in a flask containing anti-bumping granules (small pieces that make boiling smooth and stop violent bursts of bubbling).
Step 2: The liquid with the lower boiling point boils, and its vapour passes into a water-cooled condenser (a tube that cools the vapour back to liquid).
Step 3: The vapour condenses in the condenser, which has water in at the bottom and out at the top.
Step 4: The distillate (the liquid that has condensed) is collected in a receiving flask.
Step 5: A thermometer at the side arm reads the boiling point of the liquid that is distilling.

Fractional distillation separates miscible liquids with close boiling points, using a fractionating column (a tall column that gives repeated condensing and re-boiling), e.g. ethanol (boiling point 78 °C) from water (boiling point 100 °C).
Crude oil is separated into fractions (groups of compounds with similar boiling points) by fractional distillation.
notes.tip: You may be asked to describe distillation, including why water enters the condenser at the bottom. Steam distillation is not required.

notes.b: Distillation heats liquids that may be flammable and produces vapour, so the apparatus and heat source matter as well as the method.
points: Safety: flammable liquids are heated with a heating mantle or water bath, not a naked flame, so the vapour cannot ignite.
Safety: a closed system is never heated, because the pressure would build up as the vapour expands.

Diagram: a distillation set-up with a round-bottomed flask and granules, the thermometer bulb at the side arm, a Liebig condenser (a straight condenser cooled by a water jacket) with water flow, and a receiving flask.

notes.b: Paper chromatography separates and identifies small amounts of soluble substances, such as the dyes in an ink or food colouring, or a mixture of indicators. Each substance is carried up the paper by a solvent at its own speed.
points: Step 1: Draw a pencil line near the bottom of the chromatography paper; use pencil, because ink would run.
Step 2: Put small spots of the mixture and of known substances on the line.
Step 3: Stand the paper in a little solvent in a covered container, with the solvent level below the spots, so the spots are not washed into the solvent.
Step 4: Let the solvent rise up the paper, then remove the paper and mark the solvent front (the highest point the solvent reached).
Principle: components that are more soluble in the solvent (the mobile phase, which moves) and less attracted to the paper (the stationary phase, which stays still) travel further.
Retention factor (Rf) is the distance moved by the spot divided by the distance moved by the solvent.
Components are identified by matching their spots and Rf values with those of known substances.
Diagram: a chromatogram with the pencil start line, the spots, the solvent front and the separated spots.
notes.tip: Use pencil, not ink, for the start line, and keep the solvent level below the spots. You may be asked to describe separating a mixture of indicators or dyes by chromatography. Keep to paper chromatography: GC, HPLC and TLC as analytical instruments are not on the specification.

notes.b: A separating funnel separates two immiscible liquids of different density. Immiscible liquids settle into two layers, with the denser liquid underneath.
points: Examples: oil and water, or an organic layer from an aqueous layer (a water-based layer), which is used to purify an ester.
Step 1: Pour the mixture into the separating funnel and let the layers settle.
Step 2: Remove the stopper and run off the lower, denser layer through the tap.
Step 3: Collect the upper layer separately.
Diagram: a separating funnel with two layers, the stopper and the tap labelled.

keyTerms.definition: The change of state from solid to liquid when the particles gain enough energy to move past one another.
The change of state from liquid to solid as the particles lose energy and are pulled into fixed positions.
The escape of the fastest-moving particles from the surface of a liquid at any temperature below the boiling point.
The change of state from liquid to gas throughout the liquid, at the boiling point, with bubbles of vapour forming within it.
The change of state from gas to liquid as the particles are cooled and pulled close together.
The change of state from solid directly to gas, without melting.
The change of state from gas directly to solid, without becoming a liquid.
A graph of temperature against time for a substance heated at a steady rate, with flat sections at its melting and boiling points.
A technique that separates an insoluble solid from a liquid by passing the mixture through filter paper.
The solid that remains on the filter paper after filtration.
The liquid that passes through the filter paper during filtration.
A technique that forms pure crystals by evaporating some solvent from a solution, then cooling it slowly.
A technique that separates liquids by boiling the mixture and condensing the vapour that is given off.
Distillation using a fractionating column to separate miscible liquids with close boiling points.
Describes liquids that do not mix, forming two separate layers.
A technique that separates soluble substances by the different rates at which they travel up paper in a solvent.
The solvent that carries the components up the chromatography paper.
The paper, which holds back the components according to how strongly they are attracted to it.
The distance moved by a spot divided by the distance moved by the solvent front.

questions.prompt: Use the kinetic theory to explain what happens to the particles when ice melts and when water boils, and why the temperature remains constant during each change.
questions.model: When ice melts at 0 °C, heating makes the particles vibrate more until they have enough energy to overcome some of the forces holding them in fixed positions, so they move past one another as a liquid. When water boils at 100 °C, particles throughout the liquid gain enough energy to overcome the forces between them, so they separate and form bubbles of vapour within the liquid. During each change the temperature stays constant because the energy supplied is used to overcome the forces between the particles, not to increase their kinetic energy.

questions.prompt: State two assumptions of the kinetic theory and one limitation of the model.
questions.model: Assumption 1: the particles are tiny spheres in constant, random motion. Assumption 2: collisions between particles are perfectly elastic, so no kinetic energy is lost. Limitation: real particles are not hard spheres and they do attract one another; the forces between particles, which decide melting and boiling points, are ignored by the simple gas model.

questions.prompt: Describe how you would obtain pure, dry salt crystals from a mixture of sand and salt, justifying each technique you use.
questions.model: Step 1: Add water to the mixture and stir until the salt has dissolved; sand is insoluble, so it remains as a solid. Step 2: Filter the mixture, folding filter paper into a cone in a funnel and pouring the mixture through; the sand is the residue on the paper and the salt solution is the filtrate. This technique is justified because it separates an insoluble solid from a liquid. Step 3: Heat the filtrate to evaporate the water until the salt is left; this technique is justified because the salt is soluble and does not decompose on heating. Each technique is chosen because it uses the property in which the components differ: solubility in water for the first step and insolubility for the filtration.

questions.prompt: Describe how paper chromatography can be used to separate the dyes in a food colouring and identify one of them, and state the principle on which it works.
questions.model: Step 1: Draw a pencil line near the bottom of chromatography paper. Step 2: Put a small spot of the food colouring and spots of known dyes on the line. Step 3: Stand the paper in a little solvent in a covered container, with the solvent level below the spots, and let the solvent rise. Step 4: Remove the paper and mark the solvent front. Identification: calculate the Rf of each spot as the distance moved by the spot divided by the distance moved by the solvent; a dye is identified when its spot and Rf value match those of a known dye. Principle: the components that are more soluble in the solvent (the mobile phase) and less attracted to the paper (the stationary phase) travel further up the paper, so the dyes separate.
